Main.sentence: The civil rights movement [b] was a ___E:social movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_movement)___ in the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ from 1954 to 1968 which aimed to abolish legalized ___E:racial segregation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States)___ , ___E:discrimination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_discrimination_in_the_United_States)___ , and ___E:disenfranchisement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disenfranchisement_in_the_United_States)___ in the country, which most commonly affected ___E:African Americans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans)___ .
The movement had origins in the ___E:Reconstruction era U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_era)___ in the late 19th century, and modern roots in the 1940s.

After years of ___E:nonviolent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonviolent)___ protests and ___E:civil disobedience U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_disobedience)___ campaigns, the civil rights movement achieved many of its legislative goals in the 1960s, during which it secured new protections in ___E:federal law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_law)___ for the ___E:civil rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights)___ of all Americans, including the ___E:Civil Rights Act of 1964 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964)___ and the ___E:Voting Rights Act of 1965 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voting_Rights_Act_of_1965)___ .

Following the ___E:American Civil War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War)___ (1861–1865), the three ___E:Reconstruction Amendments U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_Amendments)___ to the ___E:U.S. Constitution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Constitution)___ abolished slavery and granted citizenship to all African Americans, the majority of whom had recently been enslaved in the southern states.

During Reconstruction, African-American men in the South voted and held political office, but after 1877 they were increasingly deprived of civil rights under racist ___E:Jim Crow laws U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Crow_laws)___ (which for example ___E:banned interracial marriage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-miscegenation_laws_in_the_United_States)___ , introduced ___E:literacy tests for voters U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literacy_test)___ , and ___E:segregated schools U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_segregation_in_the_United_States)___ ) and were subjected to violence from ___E:white supremacists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_supremacy)___ during the ___E:nadir of American race relations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadir_of_American_race_relations)___ .

African Americans who moved to the North in order to improve their prospects in the ___E:Great Migration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Migration_(African_American))___ also faced barriers in employment and housing.

Legal racial discrimination was upheld by the ___E:Supreme Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States)___ in its 1896 decision in Plessy v. Ferguson , which established the doctrine of " ___E:separate but equal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separate_but_equal)___ ".

The movement for civil rights, led by figures such as ___E:W. E. B. Du Bois U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._E._B._Du_Bois)___ and ___E:Booker T. Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_T._Washington)___ , achieved few gains until after ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ .

In 1948, President ___E:Harry S. Truman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman)___ issued ___E:an executive order U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_9981)___ abolishing discrimination in the armed forces.

In 1954, the Supreme Court struck down state laws establishing ___E:racial segregation in public schools U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_segregation_in_the_United_States)___ in Brown v. Board of Education .

A mass movement for civil rights, led by ___E:Martin Luther King Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr.)___ and others, began a campaign of ___E:nonviolent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonviolent)___ protests and ___E:civil disobedience U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_disobedience)___ including the ___E:Montgomery bus boycott U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_bus_boycott)___ in 1955–1956, " ___E:sit-ins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sit-in_movement)___ " in ___E:Greensboro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greensboro_sit-ins)___ and ___E:Nashville U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville_sit-ins)___ in 1960, the ___E:Birmingham campaign U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_campaign)___ in 1963, and a march from ___E:Selma to Montgomery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selma_to_Montgomery_marches)___ in 1965. Press coverage of events such as the lynching of ___E:Emmett Till U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmett_Till)___ in 1955 and the use of fire hoses and dogs against protesters in Birmingham increased public support for the civil rights movement.

In 1963, about 250,000 people participated in the ___E:March on Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_on_Washington)___ , after which President ___E:John F. Kennedy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy)___ asked Congress to pass civil rights legislation.

Kennedy's successor, ___E:Lyndon B. Johnson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson)___ , overcame the opposition of southern politicians to pass three major laws: the ___E:Civil Rights Act of 1964 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964)___ , which prohibited discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in ___E:public accommodations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_accommodations)___ , employment, and federally assisted programs; the ___E:Voting Rights Act of 1965 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voting_Rights_Act_of_1965)___ , which outlawed discriminatory voting laws and authorized federal oversight of election law in areas with a history of voter suppression; and the ___E:Fair Housing Act of 1968 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Housing_Act_of_1968)___ , which banned housing discrimination.

The Supreme Court made further pro–civil rights rulings in cases including Browder v. Gayle (1956) and Loving v. Virginia (1967), banning segregation in public transport and striking down laws against interracial marriage.
The new civil rights laws ended most legal discrimination against African Americans, though informal racism remained.

In the mid-1960s, the ___E:Black power movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_power_movement)___ emerged, which criticized leaders of the civil rights movement for their moderate and incremental tendencies. ___E:A wave of civil unrest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghetto_riots_(1964%E2%80%931969))___ in Black communities between 1964 and 1969, which peaked in 1967 and after the ___E:assassination of King U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Martin_Luther_King_Jr.)___ in 1968, weakened support for the movement from White moderates.

Despite ___E:affirmative action U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affirmative_action)___ and other programs which expanded opportunities for Black and other minorities in the U.S. by the early 21st century, racial gaps in income, housing, education, and criminal justice continue to persist.

Before the ___E:American Civil War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War)___ , ___E:eight serving presidents had owned slaves U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_who_owned_slaves)___ , almost four million black people remained ___E:enslaved in the South U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States)___ , generally only white men with property could vote, and the ___E:Naturalization Act of 1790 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalization_Act_of_1790)___ limited U.S. citizenship to ___E:whites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_people)___ .

Following the Civil War, three constitutional amendments were passed, including the ___E:13th Amendment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution)___ (1865) that ended slavery; the ___E:14th Amendment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution)___ (1869) that gave black people citizenship, adding their total for ___E:Congressional apportionment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_congressional_apportionment)___ ; and the ___E:15th Amendment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution)___ (1870) that gave black males the right to vote (only males could vote in the U.S. at the time).

From 1865 to 1877, the United States underwent a turbulent ___E:Reconstruction era U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_era)___ during which the federal government tried to establish free labor and the ___E:civil rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights)___ of freedmen in the South after the end of slavery.

Many whites resisted the social changes, leading to the formation of insurgent movements such as the ___E:Ku Klux Klan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan)___ (KKK), whose members attacked black and white ___E:Republicans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ in order to maintain ___E:white supremacy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_supremacy)___ .
In 1871, President ___E:Ulysses S. Grant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant)___ , the U.S.
Army, and U.S.

Attorney General ___E:Amos T. Akerman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amos_T._Akerman)___ , initiated a campaign to repress the KKK under the ___E:Enforcement Acts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enforcement_Acts)___ .

Some states were reluctant to enforce the federal measures of the act. In addition, by the early 1870s, other white supremacist and insurgent ___E:paramilitary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramilitary)___ groups arose that violently opposed African-American legal equality and suffrage, intimidating and suppressing black voters, and assassinating Republican officeholders.
However, if the states failed to implement the acts, the laws allowed the ___E:Federal Government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Federal_Government)___ to get involved.
Many Republican governors were afraid of sending black militia troops to fight the Klan for fear of war.

After the ___E:disputed election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1876_United_States_presidential_election)___ of 1876, which resulted in the end of Reconstruction and the withdrawal of federal troops, whites in the South regained political control of the region's state legislatures.

They continued to intimidate and violently attack blacks before and during elections to suppress their voting, but the last African Americans were elected to Congress from the South before disenfranchisement of blacks by states throughout the region, as described below.

From 1890 to 1908, southern states passed new constitutions and laws to ___E:disenfranchise U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disfranchisement_after_Reconstruction_era)___ African Americans and many ___E:Poor Whites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poor_White)___ by creating barriers to voter registration; voting rolls were dramatically reduced as blacks and poor whites were forced out of electoral politics.

After the landmark ___E:Supreme Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court)___ case of Smith v. Allwright (1944), which prohibited ___E:white primaries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_primaries)___ , progress was made in increasing black political participation in the Rim South and ___E:Acadiana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acadiana)___ – although almost entirely in urban areas  and a few rural localities where most blacks worked outside plantations.

The status quo ante of excluding African Americans from the political system lasted in the remainder of the South, especially ___E:North Louisiana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Louisiana)___ , Mississippi and Alabama, until national civil rights legislation was passed in the mid-1960s to provide federal enforcement of constitutional voting rights.
For more than sixty years, blacks in the South were essentially excluded from politics, unable to elect anyone to represent their interests in Congress or local government.
Since they could not vote, they could not serve on local juries.
During this period, the white-dominated ___E:Democratic Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ maintained political control of the South.
With whites controlling all the seats representing the total population of the South, they had a powerful ___E:voting bloc U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voting_bloc)___ in Congress.

The ___E:Republican Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ —the "party of Lincoln" and the party to which most blacks had belonged—shrank to insignificance except in remote ___E:Unionist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Unionist)___ areas of ___E:Appalachia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachia)___ and the ___E:Ozarks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozarks)___ as black voter registration was suppressed.
The Republican ___E:lily-white movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lily-white_movement)___ also gained strength by excluding blacks.
Until 1965, the " ___E:Solid South U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_South)___ " was a one-party system under the white Democrats.
Excepting the previously noted historic Unionist strongholds the Democratic Party nomination was tantamount to election for state and local office.

In 1901, President ___E:Theodore Roosevelt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt)___ invited ___E:Booker T. Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_T._Washington)___ , president of the ___E:Tuskegee Institute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuskegee_Institute)___ , to dine at the ___E:White House U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House)___ , making him the first African American to attend an official dinner there. "The invitation was roundly criticized by southern politicians and newspapers."  Washington persuaded the president to appoint more blacks to federal posts in the South and to try to boost African-American leadership in state Republican organizations.
However, these actions were resisted by both white Democrats and white Republicans as an unwanted federal intrusion into state politics.

During the same time as African Americans were being disenfranchised, white southerners imposed ___E:racial segregation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States)___ by law. Violence against blacks increased, with numerous ___E:lynchings U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynchings)___ through the turn of the century.

The system of de jure state-sanctioned racial discrimination and oppression that emerged from the post-Reconstruction South became known as the " ___E:Jim Crow U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Crow)___ " system.

The United States Supreme Court made up almost entirely of Northerners, upheld the constitutionality of those state laws that required racial segregation in public facilities in its 1896 decision Plessy v. Ferguson , legitimizing them through the " ___E:separate but equal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separate_but_equal)___ " doctrine.

Segregation, which began with slavery, continued with Jim Crow laws, with signs used to show blacks where they could legally walk, talk, drink, rest, or eat.  For those places that were racially mixed, non-whites had to wait until all white customers were served first.

Elected in 1912, President ___E:Woodrow Wilson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson)___ gave in to demands by Southern members of his cabinet who ordered segregation of workplaces in the federal government.

The early 20th century is a period often referred to as the " ___E:nadir of American race relations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadir_of_American_race_relations)___ ", when the number of lynchings was highest.

While tensions and ___E:civil rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights)___ violations were most intense in the South, social discrimination affected African Americans in other regions as well.  At the national level, the Southern bloc controlled important committees in Congress, defeated passage of federal laws against lynching, and exercised considerable power beyond the number of whites in the South.
Characteristics of the post-Reconstruction period:
African Americans rejected this regime.

They resisted it in numerous ways and sought better opportunities through lawsuits, new organizations, political redress, and labor organizing (see the ___E:Civil rights movement (1896–1954) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement_(1896%E2%80%931954))___ ).

The ___E:National Association for the Advancement of Colored People U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Colored_People)___ (NAACP) was founded in 1909. It fought to end race discrimination through litigation, education, and lobbying efforts.

Its crowning achievement was its legal victory in the Supreme Court decision Brown v. Board of Education (1954), when the ___E:Supreme Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Court)___ ruled that segregation of public schools in the US was unconstitutional and, by implication, overturned the " ___E:separate but equal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separate_but_equal)___ " doctrine established in Plessy v. Ferguson of 1896.   Following the unanimous Supreme Court ruling, many states began to gradually integrate their schools, but some areas of the South resisted by closing public schools altogether.
The integration of Southern public libraries followed demonstrations and protests that used techniques seen in other elements of the larger civil rights movement.
This included sit-ins, beatings, and white resistance.

For example, in 1963 in the city of ___E:Anniston, Alabama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anniston,_Alabama)___ , two black ministers were brutally beaten for attempting to integrate the public library.
Though there was resistance and violence, the integration of libraries was generally quicker than the integration of other public institutions.
The situation for blacks outside the South was somewhat better (in most states they could vote and have their children educated, though they still faced discrimination in housing and jobs).

In 1900 Reverend Matthew Anderson, speaking at the annual ___E:Hampton Negro Conference U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampton_Negro_Conference)___ in Virginia, said that "...the lines along most of the avenues of wage-earning are more rigidly drawn in the North than in the South.

There seems to be an apparent effort throughout the North, especially in the cities to debar the colored worker from all the avenues of higher remunerative labor, which makes it more difficult to improve his economic condition even than in the South."  From 1910 to 1970, blacks sought better lives by migrating north and west out of the South.

A total of nearly seven million blacks left the South in what was known as the ___E:Great Migration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Migration_(African_American))___ , most during and after World War II. So many people migrated that the demographics of some previously black-majority states changed to a white majority (in combination with other developments).

The rapid influx of blacks altered the demographics of Northern and Western cities; happening at a period of expanded European, Hispanic, and Asian immigration, it added to social competition and tensions, with the new migrants and immigrants battling for a place in jobs and housing.

Reflecting social tensions after World War I, as veterans struggled to return to the workforce and labor unions were organizing, the ___E:Red Summer of 1919 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Summer)___ was marked by hundreds of deaths and higher casualties across the U.S. as a result of white race riots against blacks that took place in more than three dozen cities.
Urban problems such as crime and disease were blamed on the large influx of Southern blacks to cities in the north and west, based on stereotypes of rural southern African-Americans.

Overall, blacks in Northern and Western cities experienced ___E:systemic discrimination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism_in_the_United_States)___ in a plethora of aspects of life. Within employment, economic opportunities for blacks were routed to the lowest status and restrictive in potential mobility.

Within the housing market, stronger discriminatory measures were used in correlation to the influx, resulting in a mix of "targeted violence, ___E:restrictive covenants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restrictive_covenants)___ , ___E:redlining U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redlining)___ and ___E:racial steering U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_steering)___ ".

The Great Migration resulted in many African Americans becoming urbanized, and they began to realign from the Republican to the Democratic Party, especially because of opportunities under the ___E:New Deal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal)___ of the ___E:Franklin D. Roosevelt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt)___ administration during the Great Depression in the 1930s.

Substantially under pressure from African-American supporters who began the ___E:March on Washington Movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_on_Washington_Movement)___ , President Roosevelt issued the first federal order banning discrimination and created the ___E:Fair Employment Practice Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Employment_Practice_Committee)___ .
After both World Wars, black veterans of the military pressed for full civil rights and often led activist movements.

In 1948, President ___E:Harry Truman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Truman)___ issued ___E:Executive Order 9981 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_9981)___ , which ended ___E:segregation in the military U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States_Armed_Forces)___ .

___E:Housing segregation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_segregation)___ became a nationwide problem following the Great Migration of black people out of the South. ___E:Racial covenants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenant_(law)#Exclusionary_covenants)___ were employed by many ___E:real estate developers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate_development)___ to "protect" entire ___E:subdivisions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdivision_(land))___ , with the primary intent to keep " ___E:white U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_people)___ " neighborhoods "white".
Ninety percent of the housing projects built in the years following World War II were racially restricted by such covenants.

Cities known for their widespread use of racial covenants include ___E:Chicago U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago)___ , ___E:Baltimore U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore)___ , ___E:Detroit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit)___ , ___E:Milwaukee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee)___ ,  ___E:Los Angeles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles)___ , ___E:Seattle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle)___ , and ___E:St. Louis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis)___ .
Said premises shall not be rented, leased, or conveyed to, or occupied by, any person other than of the white or Caucasian race.
— Racial covenant for a home in Beverly Hills, California.

While many whites defended their space with violence, intimidation, or legal tactics toward black people, many other whites migrated to more racially homogeneous ___E:suburban U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suburban)___ or ___E:exurban U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exurban)___ regions, a process known as ___E:white flight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_flight)___ .

From the 1930s to the 1960s, the National Association of Real Estate Boards (NAREB) issued guidelines that specified that a realtor "should never be instrumental in introducing to a neighborhood a character or property or occupancy, members of any race or nationality, or any individual whose presence will be clearly detrimental to property values in a neighborhood." The result was the development of all-black ___E:ghettos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghettos)___ in the North and West, where much housing was older, as well as South.

The first ___E:anti-miscegenation law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-miscegenation_law)___ was passed by the ___E:Maryland General Assembly U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland_General_Assembly)___ in 1691, criminalizing ___E:interracial marriage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interracial_marriage)___ .

In a speech in ___E:Charleston, Illinois U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston,_Illinois)___ in 1858, ___E:Abraham Lincoln U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln)___ stated, "I am not, nor ever have been in favor of making voters or jurors of negroes, nor of qualifying them to hold office, nor to intermarry with white people".
By the late 1800s, 38 US states had anti-miscegenation statutes.
By 1924, the ban on interracial marriage was still in force in 29 states.

While interracial marriage had been legal in California since 1948, in 1957 actor ___E:Sammy Davis Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Davis_Jr.)___ faced a backlash for his involvement with white actress ___E:Kim Novak U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Novak)___ .
Davis briefly married a black dancer in 1958 to protect himself from mob violence.

In 1958, officers in ___E:Virginia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia)___ entered the home of ___E:Mildred and Richard Loving U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loving_v._Virginia#Plaintiffs)___ and dragged them out of bed for living together as an interracial couple, on the basis that "any white person intermarry with a colored person"— or vice versa—each party "shall be guilty of a felony" and face prison terms of five years.

Invigorated by the victory of Brown and frustrated by the lack of immediate practical effect, private citizens increasingly rejected gradualist, legalistic approaches as the primary tool to bring about ___E:desegregation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desegregation_in_the_United_States)___ .

They were faced with " ___E:massive resistance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massive_resistance)___ " in the South by proponents of racial segregation and ___E:voter suppression U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disfranchisement)___ .

In defiance, African-American activists adopted a combined strategy of ___E:direct action U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_action)___ , ___E:nonviolence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonviolence)___ , ___E:nonviolent resistance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonviolent_resistance)___ , and many events described as ___E:civil disobedience U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_disobedience)___ , giving rise to the civil rights movement of 1954 to 1968.

___E:A. Philip Randolph U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._Philip_Randolph)___ had planned a march on Washington, D.C., in 1941 to support demands for elimination of ___E:employment discrimination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Employment_discrimination)___ in the ___E:defense industry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defence_industry)___ ; he called off the march when the ___E:Roosevelt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt)___ administration met the demand by issuing ___E:Executive Order 8802 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_8802)___ , which barred racial discrimination and created an ___E:agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Employment_Practice_Committee)___ to oversee compliance with the order.

The strategy of public education, legislative lobbying, and litigation that had typified the civil rights movement during the first half of the 20th century broadened after Brown to a strategy that emphasized " ___E:direct action U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_action)___ ": boycotts, ___E:sit-ins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sit-in)___ , ___E:Freedom Rides U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_Rides)___ , marches or walks, and similar tactics that relied on mass mobilization, nonviolent resistance, standing in line, and, at times, civil disobedience.
Churches, local grassroots organizations, fraternal societies, and black-owned businesses mobilized volunteers to participate in broad-based actions.
This was a more direct and potentially more rapid means of creating change than the traditional approach of mounting court challenges used by the NAACP and others.

In 1952, the ___E:Regional Council of Negro Leadership U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Council_of_Negro_Leadership)___ (RCNL), led by ___E:T. R. M. Howard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._R._M._Howard)___ , a black surgeon, entrepreneur, and planter organized a successful boycott of gas stations in Mississippi that refused to provide restrooms for blacks.

Through the RCNL, Howard led campaigns to expose brutality by the Mississippi state highway patrol and to encourage blacks to make deposits in the black-owned Tri-State Bank of ___E:Nashville U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville)___ which, in turn, gave loans to civil rights activists who were victims of a "credit squeeze" by the ___E:White Citizens' Councils U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Citizens%27_Councils)___ .

After ___E:Claudette Colvin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudette_Colvin)___ was arrested for not giving up her seat on a ___E:Montgomery, Alabama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery,_Alabama)___ bus in March 1955, a bus boycott was considered and rejected.

But when ___E:Rosa Parks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosa_Parks)___ was arrested in December, ___E:Jo Ann Gibson Robinson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Ann_Robinson)___ of the Montgomery Women's Political Council put the bus boycott protest in motion.

Late that night, she, John Cannon (chairman of the Business Department at ___E:Alabama State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama_State_University)___ ) and others mimeographed and distributed thousands of leaflets calling for a boycott.
The eventual success of the boycott made its spokesman ___E:Martin Luther King Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr.)___ , a nationally known figure.

In 1957, King and ___E:Ralph Abernathy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Abernathy)___ , the leaders of the Montgomery Improvement Association, joined with other church leaders who had led similar boycott efforts, such as ___E:C. K. Steele U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._K._Steele)___ of Tallahassee and ___E:T. J. Jemison U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._J._Jemison)___ of Baton Rouge, and other activists such as ___E:Fred Shuttlesworth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Shuttlesworth)___ , ___E:Ella Baker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ella_Baker)___ , ___E:A. Philip Randolph U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._Philip_Randolph)___ , ___E:Bayard Rustin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayard_Rustin)___ and ___E:Stanley Levison U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Levison)___ , to form the ___E:Southern Christian Leadership Conference U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Christian_Leadership_Conference)___ (SCLC).

Under the leadership of ___E:Walter Reuther U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Reuther)___ , the ___E:United Auto Workers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Auto_Workers)___ donated $75,000 to help pay for the NAACP's efforts at the Supreme Court.

Segregation of white and colored children in public schools has a detrimental effect upon the colored children.
The impact is greater when it has the sanction of the law; for the policy of separating the races is usually interpreted as denoting the inferiority of the Negro group.
The lawyers from the NAACP had to gather plausible evidence in order to win the case of Brown vs. Board of Education .
Their method of addressing the issue of school segregation was to enumerate several arguments.
One pertained to having exposure to interracial contact in a school environment.

It was argued that interracial contact would, in turn, help prepare children to live with the pressures that society exerts in regard to race and thereby afford them a better chance of living in a democracy.
In addition, another argument emphasized how "'education' comprehends the entire process of developing and training the mental, physical and moral powers and capabilities of human beings".

___E:Risa Goluboff U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risa_Goluboff)___ wrote that the NAACP's intention was to show the Courts that African American children were the victims of school segregation and their futures were at risk. Richmond County Board of Education (1899), which had applied that standard to schools, was unconstitutional.

Secretary of State ___E:Dean Acheson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_Acheson)___ was quoted in the brief stating that "The United States is under constant attack in the foreign press, over the foreign radio, and in such international bodies as the United Nations because of various practices of discrimination in this country."

Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, Kansas (1954) did not overturn Plessy v. Ferguson (1896).
Plessy v. Ferguson was segregation in transportation modes.
Brown v. Board of Education dealt with segregation in education.
Brown v. Board of Education did set in motion the future overturning of 'separate but equal'.

Even in Greensboro, much local resistance to desegregation continued, and in 1969, the federal government found the city was not in compliance with the 1964 Civil Rights Act. Transition to a fully integrated school system did not begin until 1971.

Many Northern cities also had ___E:de facto segregation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation#United_States)___ policies, which resulted in a vast gulf in educational resources between black and white communities.

In ___E:Harlem U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_(Manhattan))___ , New York, for example, neither a single new school was built since the turn of the century, nor did a single nursery school exist – even as the ___E:Second Great Migration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Great_Migration_(African_American))___ was causing overcrowding.
Existing schools tended to be dilapidated and staffed with inexperienced teachers.

Brown helped stimulate activism among ___E:New York City U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City)___ parents like ___E:Mae Mallory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mae_Mallory)___ who, with the support of the NAACP, initiated a successful lawsuit against the city and state on Brown 's principles.

The city responded to the campaign by permitting more open transfers to high-quality, historically white schools. (New York's African-American community, and Northern desegregation activists generally, now found themselves contending with the problem of ___E:white flight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_flight)___ , however.)

___E:Emmett Till U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmett_Till)___ , a 14-year-old African American from Chicago, visited his relatives in ___E:Money, Mississippi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money,_Mississippi)___ , for the summer.
He allegedly had an interaction with a white woman, Carolyn Bryant, in a small grocery store that violated the norms of Mississippi culture, and Bryant's husband Roy and his half-brother J. W.

Three days later, Till's body was discovered and retrieved from the river.

Till's mother then had his body taken back to Chicago where she had it displayed in an open casket during the funeral services where many thousands of visitors arrived to show their respects.

A later publication of an image at the funeral in Jet is credited as a crucial moment in the civil rights era for displaying in vivid detail the violent racism that was being directed at black people in America.

The state of Mississippi tried two defendants, but they were speedily acquitted by an ___E:all-white jury U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-white_jury)___ .

The murder and resulting trial ended up markedly impacting the views of several young black activists.  ___E:Joyce Ladner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyce_Ladner)___ referred to such activists as the "Emmett Till generation." Parks later informed Till's mother that her decision to stay in her seat was guided by the image she still vividly recalled of Till's brutalized remains.

The glass topped casket that was used for Till's Chicago funeral was found in a cemetery garage in 2009. Till had been reburied in a different casket after being exhumed in 2005.  Till's family decided to donate the original casket to the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American Culture and History, where it is now on display.
In 2007, Bryant said that she had fabricated the most sensational part of her story in 1955.

On December 1, 1955, nine months after a 15-year-old high school student, ___E:Claudette Colvin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudette_Colvin)___ , refused to give up her seat to a white passenger on a public bus in Montgomery, Alabama, and was arrested, ___E:Rosa Parks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosa_Parks)___ did the same thing.
Parks soon became the symbol of the resulting Montgomery bus boycott and received national publicity.
She was later hailed as the "mother of the civil rights movement".

Parks was secretary of the Montgomery NAACP chapter and had recently returned from a meeting at the ___E:Highlander Folk School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highlander_Research_and_Education_Center)___ in Tennessee where nonviolence as a strategy was taught by ___E:Myles Horton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myles_Horton)___ and others.
After Parks' arrest, African Americans gathered and organized the Montgomery bus boycott to demand a bus system in which passengers would be treated equally.
The organization was led by Jo Ann Robinson, a member of the Women's Political Council who had been waiting for the opportunity to boycott the bus system.
Following Rosa Parks' arrest, Jo Ann Robinson mimeographed 52,500 leaflets calling for a boycott.
They were distributed around the city and helped gather the attention of civil rights leaders.
After the city rejected many of its suggested reforms, the NAACP, led by ___E:E. D. Nixon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Nixon)___ , pushed for full desegregation of public buses.

This movement also sparked riots leading up to the ___E:1956 Sugar Bowl U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1956_Sugar_Bowl)___ .
In November 1956, the United States Supreme Court upheld a district court ruling in the case of Browder v. Gayle and ordered Montgomery's buses desegregated, ending the boycott.

Local leaders established the Montgomery Improvement Association to focus their efforts. ___E:Martin Luther King Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr.)___ was elected President of this organization.

The lengthy protest attracted national attention for him and the city. His eloquent appeals to Christian brotherhood and American idealism created a positive impression on people both inside and outside the South.

The Little Rock Nine were a group of nine students who attended segregated black high schools in ___E:Little Rock U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Rock,_Arkansas)___ , the capital of the state of Arkansas.

They each volunteered when the NAACP and the national civil rights movement obtained federal court orders to integrate the prestigious ___E:Little Rock Central High School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Rock_Central_High_School)___ in September, 1957. The Nine faced intense harassment and threats of violence from white parents and students, as well as organized white supremacy groups.

The enraged opposition emphasized miscegenation as the threat to white society. ___E:Arkansas Governor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Arkansas)___ , ___E:Orval Faubus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orval_Faubus)___ , claiming his only goal was to preserve the peace, deployed the Arkansas National Guard to prevent the black students from entering the school.
Faubus defied federal court orders, whereupon President Dwight D. Eisenhower intervened.

He federalized the Arkansas National Guard and sent them home. Then he sent in an elite Army unit to escort the students to school and protect them between classes during the 1957–58 school year. In class, however, the Nine were teased and ridiculed every day. In the city compromise efforts all failed and political tensions continued to fester.
A year later in September 1958 the Supreme Court ruled that all the city's high schools had to be integrated immediately.
Governor Faubus and the legislature responded by immediately shutting down all the public high schools in the city for the entire 1958–1959 school year, despite the harm it did to all the students.

The decision to integrate the school was a landmark event in the civil rights movement, and the students' bravery and determination in the face of violent opposition is remembered as a key moment in American history.
The city and state were entangled in very expensive legal disputes for decades, while suffering a reputation for hatred and obstruction.
During the time period considered to be the "African-American civil rights" era, the predominant use of protest was nonviolent, or peaceful.
Often referred to as pacifism, the method of nonviolence is considered to be an attempt to impact society positively.
Although acts of racial discrimination have occurred historically throughout the United States, perhaps the most violent regions have been in the former Confederate states.
During the 1950s and 1960s, the nonviolent protesting of the civil rights movement caused definite tension, which gained national attention.
In order to prepare for protests physically and psychologically, demonstrators received training in nonviolence.
According to former civil rights activist Bruce Hartford, there are two main components of nonviolence training.

There is the philosophical method, which involves understanding the method of nonviolence and why it is considered useful, and there is the tactical method, which ultimately teaches demonstrators "how to be a protestor—how to sit-in, how to picket, how to defend yourself against attack, giving training on how to remain cool when people are screaming racist insults into your face and pouring stuff on you and hitting you" (Civil Rights Movement Archive).

The philosophical basis of the practice of nonviolence in the American civil rights movement was largely inspired by ___E:Mahatma Gandhi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi)___ 's ___E:"non-cooperation" policies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-cooperation_movement_(1919%E2%80%9322))___ during his involvement in the ___E:Indian independence movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_independence_movement)___ , which were intended to gain attention so that the public would either "intervene in advance" or "provide public pressure in support of the action to be taken" (Erikson, 415).
As Hartford explains it, philosophical nonviolence training aims to "shape the individual person's attitude and mental response to crises and violence" (Civil Rights Movement Archive).

Hartford and activists like him, who trained in tactical nonviolence, considered it necessary in order to ensure physical safety, instill discipline, teach demonstrators how to demonstrate, and form mutual confidence among demonstrators (Civil Rights Movement Archive).
For many, the concept of nonviolent protest was a way of life, a culture.
However, not everyone agreed with this notion.

James Forman, former ___E:SNCC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_Nonviolent_Coordinating_Committee)___ (and later Black Panther) member, and nonviolence trainer was among those who did not. In his autobiography, The Making of Black Revolutionaries , Forman revealed his perspective on the method of nonviolence as "strictly a tactic, not a way of life without limitations." Similarly, ___E:Bob Moses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Moses_(activist))___ , who was also an active member of ___E:SNCC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_Nonviolent_Coordinating_Committee)___ , felt that the method of nonviolence was practical.

When interviewed by author Robert Penn Warren, Moses said "There's no question that he ( ___E:Martin Luther King Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr.)___ ) had a great deal of influence with the masses.
But I don't think it's in the direction of love. It's in a practical direction … ." (Who Speaks for the Negro?
Warren).

According to a 2020 study in the American Political Science Review , nonviolent civil rights protests boosted vote shares for the Democratic party in presidential elections in nearby counties, but violent protests substantially boosted white support for Republicans in counties near to the violent protests.

In July 1958, the ___E:NAACP Youth Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP_Youth_Council)___ sponsored sit-ins at the lunch counter of a ___E:Dockum Drug Store U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dockum_Drug_Store_sit-in)___ in downtown ___E:Wichita, Kansas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita,_Kansas)___ .
After three weeks, the movement successfully got the store to change its policy of segregated seating, and soon afterward all Dockum stores in Kansas were desegregated.

This movement was quickly followed in the same year by a ___E:student sit-in at a Katz Drug Store U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katz_Drug_Store_sit-in)___ in ___E:Oklahoma City U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City)___ led by ___E:Clara Luper U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clara_Luper)___ , which also was successful.

Mostly black students from area colleges led a sit-in at a ___E:Woolworth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._W._Woolworth_Company)___ 's store in ___E:Greensboro, North Carolina U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greensboro,_North_Carolina)___ .

On February 1, 1960, four students, ___E:Ezell A. Blair Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezell_A._Blair_Jr.)___ , David Richmond, ___E:Joseph McNeil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_McNeil)___ , and ___E:Franklin McCain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_McCain)___ from ___E:North Carolina Agricultural & Technical College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_Agricultural_and_Technical_State_University)___ , an all-black college, sat down at the segregated lunch counter to protest Woolworth's policy of excluding African Americans from being served food there.
The four students purchased small items in other parts of the store and kept their receipts, then sat down at the lunch counter and asked to be served.
After being denied service, they produced their receipts and asked why their money was good everywhere else at the store, but not at the lunch counter.

The protesters had been encouraged to dress professionally, to sit quietly, and to occupy every other stool so that potential white sympathizers could join in. The Greensboro sit-in was quickly followed by other sit-ins in ___E:Richmond, Virginia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond,_Virginia)___ ;   ___E:Nashville, Tennessee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee)___ ; and Atlanta, Georgia.

The most immediately effective of these was in Nashville, where hundreds of well organized and highly disciplined college students ___E:conducted sit-ins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville_sit-ins)___ in coordination with a boycott campaign.

As students across the south began to "sit-in" at the lunch counters of local stores, police and other officials sometimes used brutal force to physically escort the demonstrators from the lunch facilities.

The "sit-in" technique was not new—as far back as 1939, African-American attorney ___E:Samuel Wilbert Tucker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wilbert_Tucker)___ organized a sit-in at the then-segregated ___E:Alexandria, Virginia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria,_Virginia)___ , library.
In 1960 the technique succeeded in bringing national attention to the movement.

On March 9, 1960, an ___E:Atlanta University Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_University_Center)___ group of students released ___E:An Appeal for Human Rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Appeal_for_Human_Rights)___ as a full-page advertisement in newspapers, including the Atlanta Constitution , Atlanta Journal , and Atlanta Daily World .

Known as the ___E:Committee on Appeal for Human Rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Committee_on_Appeal_for_Human_Rights)___ (COAHR), the group initiated the ___E:Atlanta Student Movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Student_Movement)___ and began to lead sit-ins starting on March 15, 1960.   By the end of 1960, the process of sit-ins had spread to every southern and ___E:border state U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_states_(American_Civil_War))___ , and even to facilities in ___E:Nevada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada)___ , ___E:Illinois U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois)___ , and ___E:Ohio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio)___ that discriminated against blacks.
Demonstrators focused not only on lunch counters but also on parks, beaches, libraries, theaters, museums, and other public facilities.

In April 1960 activists who had led these sit-ins were invited by SCLC activist ___E:Ella Baker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ella_Baker)___ to hold a conference at ___E:Shaw University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaw_University)___ , a ___E:historically black university U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically_black_university)___ in ___E:Raleigh, North Carolina U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raleigh,_North_Carolina)___ .
This conference led to the formation of the ___E:Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_Nonviolent_Coordinating_Committee)___ (SNCC).
SNCC took these tactics of nonviolent confrontation further, and organized the freedom rides.

As the constitution protected interstate commerce, they decided to challenge segregation on interstate buses and in public bus facilities by putting interracial teams on them, to travel from the North through the segregated South.

Freedom Rides were journeys by civil rights activists on interstate buses into the segregated southern United States to test the United States Supreme Court decision Boynton v. Virginia (1960), which ruled that segregation was unconstitutional for passengers engaged in interstate travel.

Organized by ___E:CORE U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_Racial_Equality)___ , the first Freedom Ride of the 1960s left Washington D.C. on May 4, 1961, and was scheduled to arrive in New Orleans on May 17.

During the first and subsequent Freedom Rides, activists traveled through the ___E:Deep South U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_South)___ to integrate seating patterns on buses and desegregate bus terminals, including restrooms and water fountains.
That proved to be a dangerous mission.

In ___E:Anniston, Alabama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anniston,_Alabama)___ , one bus ___E:was firebombed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anniston_and_Birmingham_bus_attacks)___ , forcing its passengers to flee for their lives.

In ___E:Birmingham, Alabama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama)___ , an ___E:FBI U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation)___ informant reported that Public Safety Commissioner ___E:Eugene "Bull" Connor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_%22Bull%22_Connor)___ gave Ku Klux Klan members fifteen minutes to attack an incoming group of freedom riders before having police "protect" them. The riders were severely beaten "until it looked like a bulldog had got a hold of them." ___E:James Peck U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Peck_(pacifist))___ , a white activist, was beaten so badly that he required fifty stitches to his head.
In a similar occurrence in Montgomery, Alabama, the Freedom Riders followed in the footsteps of Rosa Parks and rode an integrated Greyhound bus from Birmingham.
Although they were protesting interstate bus segregation in peace, they were met with violence in Montgomery as a large, white mob attacked them for their activism.
They caused an enormous, 2-hour long riot which resulted in 22 injuries, five of whom were hospitalized.
Mob violence in Anniston and Birmingham temporarily halted the rides.
SNCC activists from Nashville brought in new riders to continue the journey from Birmingham to New Orleans.

In Montgomery, Alabama, at the ___E:Greyhound Bus Station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greyhound_Bus_Station_(Montgomery,_Alabama))___ , a mob charged another busload of riders, knocking ___E:John Lewis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lewis)___  unconscious with a crate and smashing Life photographer ___E:Don Urbrock U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Don_Urbrock&action=edit&redlink=1)___ in the face with his own camera.

A dozen men surrounded ___E:James Zwerg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Zwerg)___ ,  a white student from ___E:Fisk University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisk_University)___ , and beat him in the face with a suitcase, knocking out his teeth.

On May 24, 1961, the freedom riders continued their rides into ___E:Jackson, Mississippi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi)___ , where they were arrested for "breaching the peace" by using "white only" facilities.
New Freedom Rides were organized by many different organizations and continued to flow into the South.
As riders arrived in Jackson, they were arrested.
By the end of summer, more than 300 had been jailed in Mississippi.
… When the weary Riders arrive in Jackson and attempt to use "white only" restrooms and lunch counters they are immediately arrested for Breach of Peace and Refusal to Obey an Officer.

Says Mississippi Governor ___E:Ross Barnett U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Barnett)___ in defense of segregation: "The Negro is different because God made him different to punish him." From lockup, the Riders announce "Jail No Bail"—they will not pay fines for unconstitutional arrests and illegal convictions—and by staying in jail they keep the issue alive.
Each prisoner will remain in jail for 39 days, the maximum time they can serve without losing their right to appeal the unconstitutionality of their arrests, trials, and convictions.
After 39 days, they file an appeal and post bond...
The jailed freedom riders were treated harshly, crammed into tiny, filthy cells and sporadically beaten.

In Jackson, some male prisoners were forced to do hard labor in 100 °F (38 °C) heat. Others were transferred to the ___E:Mississippi State Penitentiary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_State_Penitentiary)___ at Parchman, where they were treated to harsh conditions.
Sometimes the men were suspended by "wrist breakers" from the walls.
Typically, the windows of their cells were shut tight on hot days, making it hard for them to breathe.

Public sympathy and support for the freedom riders led ___E:John F. Kennedy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy)___ 's administration to order the ___E:Interstate Commerce Commission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_Commerce_Commission)___ (ICC) to issue a new desegregation order.
